prompt.context: The salted food division at Nabisco has been steadily losing market share over the past two years, from a high of 20% to the current level of 18%. Profits as a percentage of sales, however, have been growing.
prompt.question: What could be causing this?

clarifying_info.a: The largest competitors are two multinational consumer products companies that feature complete lines of snack foods. Together they hold about 50% of market share.

clarifying_info.q: How does Nabisco differentiate itself from competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Nabisco's sales reps are regarded as the best in the industry.
No change in the product line.

clarifying_info.q: Why was the sales force cut?
clarifying_info.a: The sales force was cut to reduce costs, but the number of outlets remains unchanged.

clarifying_info.q: What caused the change in the marketing budget?
clarifying_info.a: The changes come from reduced trade promotions.
Products are primarily sold in large grocery store chains and convenience stores.

clarifying_info.q: How often does the sales force visit customers?
clarifying_info.a: The sales force visits each customer at least once per quarter.
Promotions usually occur at the end of each quarter.

clarifying_info.q: What is the impact of promotions?
clarifying_info.a: Promotions are required for end-of-aisle displays and advertising space.

framework: External Factors - Competitor dynamics: have existing players grown share or have new entrants arrived?
External Factors - Market dynamics: is the total market growing and is Nabisco capturing that growth?
Internal Factors: assess whether the company is spending adequately on promotions and sales force to maintain shelf presence
Internal Factors: examine cost structure changes that explain rising profit margins despite share loss
Synthesize: connect cost reductions (sales force, trade promotions) to operational outcomes (shelf space, market share)

questions.prompt: Review Exhibits 1 and 2. What do they tell you about Nabisco sales performance relative to the market?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate will note that Nabisco absolute sales may be growing, but the total market is growing faster, hence the market share decline from 20% to 18%. This distinguishes a revenue-share problem from an absolute revenue problem.

math.setup: If the market is growing and Nabisco share fell from 20% to 18%, Nabisco sales grew more slowly than the market.
steps: Market grew faster than Nabisco own sales
math.answer: Market growth outpaced Nabisco sales growth, causing a 2 percentage-point share decline.

questions.prompt: Review Exhibit 3. What changes in cost structure stand out, and what might they signal?
questions.guidance: The candidate should highlight the decline in Sales force spend (9% to 7%) and Marketing spend (18% to 16%), while Pre-tax profit improved (14% to 17%). The candidate should hypothesize that cost cuts caused the market share loss and ask follow-up questions about trade promotions and sales force coverage.

math.setup: Compare each cost line current % vs two-years-ago %
math.answer: Profit margin rose 3pp while sales force and marketing each fell about 2pp, suggesting cost savings came at the expense of market-facing investment.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the potential consequences of reducing trade promotions and sales force size in a grocery and convenience store channel?

categories.name: Shelf Space and Visibility
ideas: Competitors filling vacated premium shelf positions

categories.name: Retailer Relationships
ideas: Weaker retailer loyalty without promotional support
Less negotiating leverage for prime placement
Reduced co-op advertising with retail partners

categories.name: Consumer Reach
ideas: Lower brand visibility at point of sale
Consumers substituting competitor brands in promotionally driven category

categories.name: Sales Force Impact
ideas: Fewer quarterly visits means delayed issue detection
Reduced ability to secure new product placement
Less face time to negotiate promotional calendars

recommendation: Nabisco market share decline is driven by cuts to the sales force and trade promotions, which are critical for securing shelf space and end-of-aisle displays in grocery and convenience channels
While profitability has improved short term (pre-tax margin up from 14% to 17%), this is not sustainable if share continues to erode and the growing market is captured by competitors
Recommendation: reinvest selectively in trade promotions and restore sales force visit frequency, especially as the market is growing and the product line has not changed
risks: Profitability may decline in the short term as promotional and sales force costs are reinstated
Competitors who gained shelf space during the cutback may resist giving it back
Market share may continue to slip before promotional investment takes effect
next_steps: Conduct a shelf-space audit across key grocery chain and convenience store accounts to quantify lost placement
Model the incremental revenue from recovering 1 to 2 percentage points of market share versus the cost of restored promotions
Explore whether new product extensions could capture growth in the expanding market while shelf presence is rebuilt
